April 29, 2025
RE: LD854 - An Act to Provide Equitable Capital Construction Funding for Maine's Charter Schools
My name is Douglass Moore, and I live in Sabattus. I am testifying in opposition to LD854.
On its surface, this bill appears simple -- a technical amendment to a definition. But in practice, it threatens to undermine the already underfunded public school districts that serve the vast majority of Maine students.
Maine's Public Schools Are Already Struggling to Keep Up
Across the state, public schools are grappling with rising costs due to inflation -- not just for fuel and food, but for essential classroom supplies and building maintenance. Teacher salaries in many districts have failed to keep pace with the cost of living, and worsening teacher-to-student ratios are stretching resources thinner every year. In some counties, such as Kennebec, school boards have even begun touting these cuts as signs of efficiency -- a deeply troubling trend when the reality is our students are being shortchanged.
Charter Schools Should Not Compete for Public Construction Funds
Public charter schools in Maine are often managed by private boards, and they do not answer to locally elected school committees. They already operate with greater flexibility and reduced accountability -- and now this bill seeks to make them eligible for the same pot of construction funding that our town-run public schools depend on. This would divert critical resources from districts that are required to serve all students, regardless of need, disability status, or background.
A Step Toward Privatization
Make no mistake -- this bill fits into a broader national effort to blur the line between public schools and charter schools in order to normalize privatization. If passed, it sets a precedent for further legislative efforts to equalize public and charter school funding -- without equal oversight or responsibility. That's not reform. That's erosion.
This Bill Ignores the Rural Reality of Maine
Unlike urban or suburban areas, most Maine towns -- including my own -- do not have access to charter schools. The families in these communities rely entirely

on our local public schools, and any state dollars siphoned away from them hurts us directly. If this bill passes, rural districts will be forced to compete for state funds with schools that do not even serve their communities.
No Oversight, No Equity, No Guardrails
LD 1517 includes no mechanisms to ensure that charter school construction projects prioritize equity, address high-need areas, or even align with local planning goals. It is a blank check -- and the students in our public schools will be left holding the bill.
Conclusion
Maine should be investing more in its public school infrastructure, not diluting that investment by expanding eligibility to institutions that do not serve the public in the same way. I urge the committee to reject LD 1517 and instead prioritize the needs of the public school students who rely on us to provide safe, well-funded learning environments.
Thank you for your time and for your service to Maine's students.

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 854
AN ACT TO PROVIDE EQUITABLE CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION FUNDING FOR MAINE'S CHARTER SCHOOLS
May 6, 2025
Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and members of the Education and Cultural Affairs Committee, I am Eileen King, the Deputy Executive Director for Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association in opposition to L.D. 854, which proposes to extend school construction funding to charter schools in Maine. While we acknowledge the importance of providing quality learning environments for all students, this bill raises several concerns that we believe must be addressed.
Maine has over 400 public school buildings constructed before 1990, many of which are in dire need of repair. The state's public schools are facing critical infrastructure issues, with aging buildings that require significant investment to maintain a safe and functional learning environment.
The conditions of our schools have raised such concern that a special commission has been created to study the issue, underscoring the urgency of addressing these challenges.
Given the severity of the situation, we are deeply concerned that the funding proposed in L.D. 854 would further strain already limited resources. The current state funding supports only 5-7 school construction projects every four years, which is woefully inadequate in addressing the overwhelming needs across the state. Public schools are simply not receiving the support necessary to modernize and repair their aging facilities which ultimately impact our children's learning environments.
Furthermore, the revolving renovation funds currently available to schools are insufficient to address even most of our school's repair needs. These funds fall far short of the amount needed to effectively manage the aging infrastructure that many schools are grappling with.
It is vital that we first address the urgent needs of our current public-school buildings. The focus of our limited resources should be on ensuring that the majority of Maine's students, who attend public schools, have access to safe and modern learning environments.
We urge the committee to oppose this bill and to prioritize the substantial infrastructure needs of Maine's public schools. Our students deserve better than to continue learning in buildings that are falling apart, and funding should be directed towards the schools that face the most significant challenges.

Steven W. Bailey
MSBA Executive Director

Eileen E. King
MSSA Executive Director
10050184:
Testimony in Support of LD 854: "An Act to Provide Equitable Capital Construction Funding for Maine's Charter Schools"
Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free-market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in support of LD 854, "An Act to Provide Equitable Capital Construction Funding for Maine's Charter Schools."
This bill represents a long-overdue correction to a glaring inequity in Maine's education funding system. Public charter schools serve more than 2,700 students from many municipalities across Maine, offering families high-quality, flexible educational options that meet the needs of diverse learners.1 Yet despite their status as public schools, charter schools are denied access to critical state funding for capital construction--a fundamental resource that traditional school districts rely on to build and maintain safe, functional learning environments.
LD 854 addresses this disparity by amending 20-A MRSA �15901 to explicitly include public charter schools among the school administrative units eligible for school construction funding. This change is not only fair--it is essential. Denying charter schools access to construction funds creates a two-tiered public education system in which some schools receive full support from the state. In contrast, others are forced to scrape together private dollars for essential infrastructure needs. This undermines the principles of equity and accountability that Maine's education system purports to uphold.
Maine's charter schools already operate under strict performance standards, which are, in fact, far more stringent than those of other public schools. Additionally, they have regular evaluations and the ever-present risk of closure if results are not met. Compared to traditional public schools, charter schools serve a higher proportion of low-income and disadvantaged students, often with fewer resources. Yet, charter schools consistently demonstrate strong academic results, parent satisfaction, and fiscal responsibility.
The current policy effectively penalizes charter schools for their independence. Traditional school districts are free to raise local funds and receive state support for capital needs, while charter schools, prohibited from levying taxes, must resort to
1 https://www.govtech.com/education/k-12/ten-years-on-maines-charter-schools-yield-mixed-results

fundraising or lease arrangements to provide basic facilities.2 This creates a serious and unnecessary barrier to growth and innovation in Maine's public education system. As noted in the Maine Policy Institute's 2025 Legislative Guidebook, "Charter schools utilize fewer resources than traditional public schools and serve a higher percentage of lower-income and minority students," yet are held to higher standards and denied essential funding streams.3 This is indefensible. By passing LD 854, the Legislature would affirm that all public school students deserve equitable access to safe, modern learning environments regardless of whether they attend a traditional district or a charter school. We urge this committee to support LD 854, which promotes fairness, equality, student opportunity, and educational excellence. Thank you for your time and consideration.
